segments.text: Part 3. You will hear two business students discussing a case study about a small bakery for a report they are writing together. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.
That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers.

part.title: A bakery case study

turns.text: Right, Callum, shall we make a start on the bakery case study? The report's due on Friday.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Yeah, good idea. I've read it twice now. Shall we begin with what Hartley's Bakery got right?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: OK. At first I thought the loyalty card was one of their strengths, but then I noticed they gave it up after about three months, because hardly anyone used it.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Right, so that doesn't really count. What about the location? It's near the station, isn't it?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Well, it's on a side street behind the station, so most commuters walk straight past it. If anything, I'd put that under problems.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Fair enough. And staff training? I thought they had a proper programme.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: The owner talks about wanting one, but it never actually happened. They just learn on the job.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: OK. For me, the real strength is where everything comes from. All their flour is milled about five miles away and the eggs come from a farm nearby. And then there's Instagram: the owner posts photos of the morning bake every day, and that's what brings in most new customers.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Agreed, those are the two to focus on. So, problems. The case study mentions that big supermarket that opened on the ring road last year.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Yes, but the owner says her sales hardly changed after it opened, so I don't think that's a real issue. And the online reviews are nearly all five stars, so it's not about quality either.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: No. What struck me was the bills. Running the ovens from four in the morning means their electricity costs have almost doubled in two years. And then there's how much they throw away. Around a fifth of everything they bake is still on the shelves at closing time.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: That's a lot. I'd expected them to say they couldn't find trained bakers, but apparently recruitment has been easy.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Right. So what are we going to recommend? I wondered about moving to the high street, where more people pass by.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: The rent there's three times as much, though. They'd never afford it. What about staying open into the evening?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That means paying staff for extra hours, and the area's pretty quiet after six. I don't think so.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: So I'd go for two things. First, replacing the old ovens with energy-efficient ones. There's a government grant that would cover half the cost. Second, selling whatever's left at the end of the day at half price, maybe through one of those food-waste apps.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Yes, that tackles both of the big problems directly. Should we suggest a marketing consultant as well?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I don't think they need one. Their Instagram's already doing that job for free.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: True. OK, the second section is what to do with each product. Let's start with the sourdough.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.say: It's their bestseller. It sells out by eleven most mornings, and at three pounds twenty a loaf it's cheaper than anywhere else in town.
turns.text: It's their bestseller. It sells out by eleven most mornings, and at £3.20 a loaf it's cheaper than anywhere else in town.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: I was going to say they should just bake more of it, but that means more energy. I reckon they could easily charge more, and people would still buy it.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Agreed. Next, the cinnamon buns. They fly off the shelves on Saturdays and Sundays, but from Monday to Friday nearly half of them end up in the bin.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: So should they stop making them altogether?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: No, they're far too popular for that. They should just bake them for the weekend and leave them out the rest of the time.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Makes sense. Then there are the celebration cakes. At the moment you have to go into the shop to order one, and the owner admits she loses customers because of that.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I'd thought about suggesting an advert in the local paper, but that's a bit old-fashioned. People want to choose a design and pay from home, so they should set up a way to order them through the website.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Good. Sandwiches next. They're really the part of the business that loses money. The fillings have to be bought fresh every day, there's the café next door competing, and they make about 10p on each one.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I was going to say cut the price, but you're right, there's no point. Let's just say they should stop making them completely.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: What about the gluten-free brownies? Hardly anyone buys them in the shop.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: No, but the case study says two cafés in town have asked about stocking them. So instead of relying on the shop, they could sell them to cafés and offices in the area.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That's better than my idea, which was just to change the packaging. And the meat pies?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: They're a bit tricky. They make thirty a day, but only about twenty get sold. They're worth keeping, but they should make fewer of them.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.say: And finally, the hot drinks. A coffee's only one pound fifty, which is about a pound less than the chains charge.
turns.text: And finally, the hot drinks. A coffee's only £1.50, which is about a pound less than the chains charge.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I'd say leave those as they are. Actually, no. The beans come from a local roaster, so customers would happily pay a bit more. Let's put that down too.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Right. I'll write up the products section tonight and send it over tomorrow, Callum.
turns.speaker: student_a

questions.evidence: They're worth keeping, but they should make fewer of them.

explanation.uk: З тридцяти пирогів щодня продається лише близько двадцяти, тому пироги варто залишити, але пекти їх менше.
